Memory × Reflection × Persistence in Dementia

How do concepts of memory, reflection and persistence relate to dementia?

Dementia is a condition where these three concepts — memory, reflection, and persistence — are directly challenged and reshaped. Dementia is a progressive syndrome that alters memory, reflection (metacognition), and the persistence of experience across time. It is a major public health challenge; person‑centred care is recommended by clinical guidelines.

Memory

Core impairment in dementia is the degradation of episodic memory (events, experiences) and later semantic memory (knowledge). The conceptual cycle of Select, Change, Reconstruct — becomes unstable:

  • Select: Attention narrows, reducing what can be encoded in the first place.
  • Change: Consolidation fails; synaptic traces are not stabilized.
  • Reconstruct: Recall becomes fragmentary, with gaps filled by confabulation (false but plausible memories).

Reflection

Reflection means the ability to step back, introspect, and interpret one’s experiences. Dementia disrupts metacognition (awareness of one’s own memory state):

  • Early dementia: people may notice and reflect on lapses.
  • Later stages: anosognosia (lack of awareness of deficits) emerges, limiting self-reflection.

Families often become the “external reflection” — helping the person contextualize identity when self-reflection falters.

Persistence

Dementia undermines persistence at multiple levels:

  • Neural persistence: Synaptic traces are lost due to neurodegeneration (amyloid plaques, tau tangles).
  • Experiential persistence: Memories no longer endure across time; conversations and events fade rapidly.
  • Identity persistence: Without durable memory, continuity of self weakens. John Locke’s idea of personal identity via memory continuity is directly challenged in dementia.

Interactions

  • Memory × Reflection: The inability to reflect on lost memories accelerates disorientation; reflection depends on persistent memory.
  • Memory × Persistence: Loss of persistence means every moment risks becoming ephemeral, producing “living in the present” but without stable anchoring.
  • Reflection × Persistence: As persistence fades, reflection becomes hollow — like trying to reflect in a mirror that no longer holds an image.

Implications

  • Clinical: Therapies often aim to scaffold persistence (e.g., memory books, environmental cues) and enable reflection externally (life-story work, reminiscence therapy).
  • Philosophical: Dementia illustrates the fragility of self-continuity. It shows that memory is not just information, but the persistence of narrative identity.
  • Artistic/Experiential: Projects using layered images, composites, or fading overlays can metaphorically represent dementia’s erosion of memory, reflection, and persistence.
Phase In Dementia Supportive Interventions
Select Narrowed attention/encoding; fewer events become durable memories. Offer CST; optimise sensory inputs (vision/hearing), daylight, sleep, exercise; simplify environments and prompts.
Change Consolidation/reconsolidation weakened by synaptic dysfunction and neurodegeneration. Consistent routines; structured reminiscence; life‑story books to stabilise autobiographical schema; carer training.
Reconstruct Retrieval is fragmentary; insight may be limited (anosognosia); identity narratives weaken. Person‑centred communication; externalised narratives (photos, labelled spaces, memory books); group engagement to co‑create meaning.
